rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is one of the most progressive in its region for trans visitors.

Legal gender recognition is available via civil registration, and a national anti-discrimination law protects gender identity. Same-sex marriage is legal from 2022, and no far-right group is in government.

No documented criminal incidents against trans visitors were found. Reporting gaps exist for such incidents.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The legal gender recognition system and the 2022 change apply to residents rather than to visitors.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: No official travel policy for trans visitors exists. General urban criminal conduct is very low.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this country is among the most progressive in its region on LGBTIQ rights — same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations able to register — with comprehensive anti-discrimination laws enacted since 2016 covering sexual orientation and gender identity.
thin: no usable finding

National interior ministry notice of 29 October 2022: the local jurisdiction step in legal gender change procedures was abolished on the recommendation of the advocate of the principle of equality, so trans persons are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of trans identity in their local environment.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: a national LGBT advocacy organisation documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and a trans advocacy organisation documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023; after the pride march, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate, the head of government took three days to react, and the interior minister made no statements.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: the national health ministry confirmed that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition and formally asked the interior ministry to amend the relevant civil registry act sub-article.

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights practices report for this country: no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and there were no reports of official-condoned violence, but authorities recorded incidents without tracking case numbers and local NGOs called violence against LGBTI persons prevalent and under-reported; in June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the pride route and marchers had eggs thrown at them.

Research institute's national report (January 2025) from an EU-funded project: civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, but LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles; the report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

Foreign news agency report of 25 July 2006: this country passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official — no friends or relatives; gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the move as a concrete step while criticising the law as 'insufficient'.

Foreign broadsheet with newswire reporting (December 2015): the leader of a major global church urged this country's politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March — the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is generally safe for trans visitors.

Same-sex marriage is legal from 2024, and a national equality plan for LGBT people exists from 2025, with focus on trans residents. Legal gender recognition has official requirements, and changes to the law have stalled.

No documented criminal incidents against trans visitors were found, and no same-sex conduct is criminalised.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The legal gender recognition system and its stalled law changes apply to residents.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: No official travel policy for trans visitors exists. General urban criminal conduct is very low.
blindSourceSummaries: National news outlet: this country approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan, developed over about two years by the equality-policies department of a national ministry; sets targets across education (inclusive curricula, physical and mental safety of LGBTIQ students and staff), healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, anchored on the principle that this country should be a great place for LGBTIQ people to live; trans-relevant: the legal framework is to be updated to support gender identity and expression protections.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): all same-sex relations legal nationwide; this country was the first in its region to achieve marriage equality (2023, including joint adoption; opposition filed hundreds of amendments to block it and failed); public support for marriage equality rose from 34% in 2012 to 53% in 2023 (75% among younger adults); a national LGBTI equal-opportunities action plan was approved in 2025 with special attention to trans wellbeing; advocacy continues for self-determination-based legal gender recognition and for hate-speech and hate-crime laws; LGBTI organisations can register.

LGBT-rights index data for this country: same-sex relations legal, marriage legal, no censorship; legal gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis; no nonbinary recognition; no hate-crime protections; employment discrimination prohibited on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds; housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only; conversion therapy not banned; bathroom access protected; residents rank first among 30 regional units for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Global transgender-rights barometer time series for this country (2011-2024): legal gender recognition exists but requires physiological alteration and psychiatric diagnosis; hate-speech and hate-crime legislation does not include gender identity; workplace, housing and healthcare anti-discrimination laws include gender identity; no known murders of gender-identity minorities.

Regional compliance report (2018) on this country's implementation of a regional human-rights body's recommendation on measures to combat discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity: covers hate crimes and data collection, safety of LGBT people deprived of liberty, hate speech, association, expression, transgender-specific health and private-life issues, employment, education, housing, sports and asylum.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2026 (covering 2025), chapter on this country: joined 16 EU states in urging reform of anti-LGBTI laws in the region; the foreign minister publicly supported the national pride and diplomatic missions flew rainbow flags; in December the country adopted a national action plan to strengthen LGBTI equality across education, healthcare, employment and the legal system.

Regional fundamental-rights agency LGBTIQ survey country sheet (2024): 62% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (regional average 53%); 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (regional average 29%); 38% are open about being LGBTIQ (regional average 51%); workplace discrimination below the regional average (12% versus 19%).

Foreign news outlet (July 2017): foreign embassies and international missions in the capital issued a joint declaration for the regional pride of 2017, affirming LGBTI rights as human rights and calling for an environment free from discrimination — external diplomatic backing for open LGBTI life in this country at a pride moment.

Local LGBTI organisation retrospective (October 2021): seven-year review of the 2014 cohabitation act — implementation gaps forced litigation: a 2016 appeal court ordered a county government to register a same-sex marriage concluded abroad, and courts repeatedly found unequal treatment unconstitutional; the half-law era ended when marriage equality passed in 2023.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is progressive in its region. Same-sex marriage is legal from 2019.

Gender markers can only be changed via legal gender recognition, with case-by-case court rulings. No documented criminal incidents against trans visitors were found, and no same-sex conduct is criminalised.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The gender-marker policy and its stalled law changes apply to residents.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: No official travel policy for trans visitors exists. General risks apply to all travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: Analysis outlet (February 2026): the 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery to change legal gender blocks an estimated 90% of trans people from obtaining matching national identity documents; every identity-document-requiring aspect of daily life becomes a potential site of distress and discrimination; the national health and welfare ministry has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013.

Analysis outlet (January 2026): the government continues to flounder on transgender rights — no tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction; pending conscription-criteria changes could actively harm trans people; anti-gender movement activity is rising, with some organisations supporting foreign anti-trans policies and a local political party calling for a 'two genders' position.

National newspaper (August 2024): the environment ministry will invest about 280 million in the national currency over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide (from 623 to 1,246 by 2029); among trans and gender-neutral survey respondents reporting discrimination, 17% of incidents occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.
National news agency (November 2025): an LGBT+ rights group finds only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.
Source note: not retrievable at research time (page removed); the underlying page addressed this country's transgender-rights law, protections and gaps.
Analysis outlet (November 2024): analysis of the wave of anti-gender discourse in this country — rising anti-gender movement activity and its political context.

News outlet (August 2024): a court denied a transgender woman's request to change the gender marker on her government-issued identity document without requiring surgery or a psychological evaluation; the supporting rights group says they will likely appeal.

Legal-news dispatch (November 2025): the seventh annual transgender march in this country drew an estimated 3,000 people despite rain, with international participants; calls for an end to discrimination against trans people continue as the rights debate continues.

Travel and resources page for this country: described as one of the most progressive countries in its region for LGBT rights; notes the country regularised adoption for same-sex parents in May 2023; lists organisations, bars, spas and venues across many cities.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is among the few that criminalise trans people as such via religious law.

Enforcement of these laws creates real risks for all trans people, with official raids on trans community events reported and the media tipped off in advance by the authorities. Political influence has grown for religious-conservative groups, and official rehabilitation programs for LGBT people exist.

For a foreign trans visitor who does not follow the country's religion, the religious offence does not apply directly, but same-sex conduct is a national criminal offence with severe penalties, applying to residents and international visitors alike. There is no legal gender recognition.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct is a national criminal offence with severe penalties, and it applies to all, including trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General risks apply to all travellers; the overall level is based on trans risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights legal organisation's country profile: the national penal code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping), alongside religious-law enactments across the state/province units prohibiting cross-dressing or males posing as females, including a 2019 religious-criminal-code enactment covering sodomy and sexual intercourse against the order of nature; situates this country among jurisdictions that criminalise, with active litigation listed alongside comparable cases elsewhere.

Human-rights organisation report (August 2022) based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across the country: every state/province maintains religious codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, and the national penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping; government-funded rehabilitation retreats had drawn hundreds of attendees by mid-2021, and LGBT events and media content were censored; one case shows enforcement reach — many religious officers were mobilised to hunt a trans woman over an 'insulting religion' charge before she fled abroad and gained international protection.

Human-rights organisation report (June 2019): a transgender woman was killed — the third such killing of a trans woman in this country in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity.

Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying newswire report (August 2023) covers growing LGBTQ fears in this country as religious-conservative groups shatter reform hopes.

Foreign policy publication (December 2025): police raided a male-only sauna in the capital and arrested over two hundred men under a national same-sex-conduct provision — the largest such raid in years — with the media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, including suspension of civil servants identified among them; a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking grounds, yet release was delayed; many remained held at one point, including foreign nationals whose embassies intervened; a rights group mobilised bailors and legal aid; days later police raided another site in another city. Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.

Source note: not retrievable at research time (DNS failure); the underlying legal case summary covers this country's high court denying a request to declare the religious cross-dressing law unconstitutional.
Source note: the regional development programme and transgender network publication on this country returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

International legal body (July 2020): a religious-affairs minister announced that a national religious department had been given full licence to carry out its enforcement actions against transgender persons; the legal body condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees. Documents official targeting of trans people in the national state/province units.

Practical travel guide (updated July 2026): national same-sex-conduct provisions criminalise carnal intercourse against the order of nature for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; religious-code offences apply only to Muslims (maximum 3 years, a fine, and strokes); the national court struck down some state/province religious provisions on division-of-powers grounds without decriminalising anything under the penal code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human-rights organisation report (September 2014): since the 1980s every state/province has passed religious enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all bar Muslim men from dressing as women and some also bar women posing as men — enforced by religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing; documents a strip-search and sexual assault of a trans woman by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over twenty times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes, and prison terms of months to years with male-ward sexual violence; follows the mass arrest of trans women at a wedding that triggered a constitutional challenge.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is broadly safe, with very low crime, no criminalisation of trans identity, and no religious police.

A law that criminalised same-sex conduct was repealed in 2022, and official prison data report no assaults on trans prisoners. Legal gender recognition requires genital surgery and is costly; no national anti-discrimination law protects gender identity, and a 2025 workplace fairness statute explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity; many trans residents report negative workplace experiences.

For visitors: official border processing is efficient, street crime is very low, bathroom access is unrestricted, and no trans-specific police friction is reported. The general atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2022 repeal of the same-sex-conduct law removed criminal exposure for trans visitors with partners.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The legal gender recognition system, the workplace fairness statute, and the workplace-experience findings apply to residents; official prison data concern resident prisoners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General criminal conduct is very low. No official travel policy for trans visitors exists.
blindSourceSummaries: Community organisation's report (February 2025): the transgender community faces several key challenges to health and well-being — the difficult process of legal gender recognition with prohibitive cost due to required genital surgeries; discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students; discrimination in the employment sector; and discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings (the claim text as captured ends mid-sentence).

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal; legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations cannot register — registration remains the structural gap despite decriminalisation.

National newspaper (November 2023): the prison service reported 10 transgender inmates currently behind bars and no recorded cases of assault against transgender inmates — a rare official datum on trans prisoners in the system.

LGBTQ community organisation (January 2025): the new workplace-fairness legislation gives this country its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it stops short of covering LGBTQ+ workers — gender identity and expression are not protected grounds, leaving workplace exposure for trans staff.
Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying report (June 2023) covers this country's LGBT community feeling safer as the end of the same-sex-conduct ban brings change.

Foreign newspaper (July 2025): a clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden lifestyles sparked calls for review — a former radio DJ and actor argued the grouping has no place after decriminalisation. Media-regulation residue after decriminalisation.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is among the most severe environments for trans people, with a unique bifurcation in official policy.

Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty, and a trans woman was raped in official custody (documented case, 2023). Trans people who have not had surgery face criminal moral and decency provisions with prison, fines and lashes, plus documented pressure to transition.

However, transsexuality is legally recognised under a 1987 fatwa, and gender-affirming surgery is government-funded — making this country one of the few in the region with legal recognition of trans identity. A post-operative trans visitor with matching documents is better positioned than a pre-operative or non-binary visitor, or anyone perceived as same-sex-active, who face the death penalty, official-custody sexual violence, and forced-transition pressure.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty — a catastrophic risk for any visitor perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The 1987 recognition of transsexuality and government-funded gender-affirming surgery apply to residents. Pressure on gay people to transition is a resident phenomenon, and it signals official policy.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General official-surveillance risks, compulsory dress law for women, and the risk of detention for foreign nationals apply to all travellers; the overall level is based on trans risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: Broadcast outlet: the capital's authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid 'busy' areas — official advisories restricting trans visibility in public space, illustrating official pressure on gender-nonconforming people in this country.
Rights organisation: an imprisoned trans rights activist's open letter recounts rape in an intelligence-ministry detention facility — documented custodial violence against trans detainees.

Community organisation submission (February 2025) to a UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity: survey of 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled the country (96% from ethnic minorities) documenting systematic persecution driving displacement.
International LGBT-rights organisation country overview: same-sex relations illegal nationwide for men and women, with the policy and legal-status matrix as baseline reference.

Foreign government's country policy and information note (December 2025): the national penal code criminalises all same-sex activity (flogging to death penalty); no discrimination protections; convictions on pretext of more severe charges; gender reassignment surgery is permitted and may be subsidised after a 'gender identity disorder' diagnosis, but is invasive and often sub-standard; recognition only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

News outlet (2025): trans medical tourism is booming in this country while transitions are forced on locals — foreign patients seek government-subsidised surgery while local trans people face pressure to conform to binary transition or face legal penalty.

Business magazine: the government funds gender-reassignment surgery but the price is dignity — analysis of how conditional tolerance coerces trans residents, with surgical pressure framed as 'protection'.

Community organisation submission to this country's universal periodic review (early 2025): human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people — documentation of persecution, violence and legal discrimination.
Human-rights organisation (November 2005): two more men executed for homosexual conduct — recorded execution practice for same-sex conduct, the enforcement backdrop for trans and LGBT visitors.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it now has one of the world's most explicitly anti-trans statutes, in force since 1 July 2024. Amendments to the 1988 anti-prostitution law criminalise same-sex relationships (10–15 years), “biological sex change based on personal desire and inclination” (criminalising transition itself), and men who “intentionally act like women” (1–3 years) — a direct statutory criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Promoting homosexuality carries a minimum 7-year sentence. The head of the nation signed the law on 29 June 2024.

Behind the statute stands a documented milieu of lethal violence: militia-led campaigns against men perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming, with impunity. Most LGBT residents hide their identity entirely. One region of the country has not passed the national law but shares the social climate and has no protections.

For a visitor: being visibly trans is a statutory offence; discovery risks 1–3 years, with severe custodial and militia risk beyond the legal penalty.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex relationships criminalised at 10–15 years under the 2024 amendments — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The 1988-law amendments apply under the national law; a suspended regional parliament has not adopted them, but no protection exists there either.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights organisation (20 May 2024): the national parliament passed (27 Apr 2024) an anti-LGBT amendment to the 1988 law on combatting prostitution — same-sex relations punishable by 10-15 years' prison, 1-3 years for undergoing or performing gender-affirming procedures; the organisation calls for repeal.

Broadcast outlet: the new law criminalises same-sex relationships with 10-15 years' jail, 1-3 years for transgender people, plus penalties for 'promoting homosexuality' — framed by supporters as upholding religious values, condemned by rights groups.

Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying national legal-library monitor entry (May 2024) documents the new law prohibiting prostitution, homosexuality and gender-change procedures.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation briefing (15 Jan 2025): on 28 Apr 2024 the country amended the 1988 prostitution law to explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression; signed by the president on 29 Jun 2024 — the operative legal baseline.

Foreign government country policy note (v3.0, July 2025): assessment of risk from official and hybrid actors and non-official actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

Foreign government 2012 human-rights report for this country: documents sectarian violence, torture, impunity, and 'societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity' — official acknowledgment of the dangers facing LGBT people in the country.

Broadcast outlet (27 Oct 2023): a prominent internet personality was fatally shot in the capital amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community — targeted killing of a visible figure as the anti-LGBT climate hardened.

Broadcast outlet investigation: dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people killed in recent years in the post-occupation country while authorities turn a blind eye — the UN says official neglect makes the country a perpetrator; documented culture of abuse and impunity for anti-LGBT violence.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors — the strongest jurisdiction in its region by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via a regional human-rights court's advisory opinion (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. The capital has a visible scene.
rewrites.blindTangential: Marriage equality since 2020 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The administrative name/photo ID process (which does not change the sex marker) and universal healthcare covering transition-related care are resident-facing.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: ID sex-marker limits and Church influence are resident-facing/climate.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct legal since 1971; first country in its region to adopt marriage equality (2020); since 2018 legal gender change on documents without surgery or court order; the national health system funds gender-affirming care; rollback pressure — a conversion-therapy bill stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
International LGBTI-rights database jurisdiction page for this country: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, gender recognition and protections.

UN health-rights rapporteur report on her July 2023 visit to this country (April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

Legal reference for this country: survivor's pension extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (a labour-ministry announcement 25 Jun 2016; individual survivor benefit approved 29 Jun 2018; teachers' separate budget excluded); also records the 2000 supreme court ruling that IVF is unconstitutional — dated partnership-benefits context.

News outlet (1 May 2008): the government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia (17 May); the president and the health minister directed public institutions to facilitate, promote and support activities 'directed at the eradication of homophobia'.

Regional news outlet (16 May 2014): the president flew the rainbow flag at the presidential residence on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May (officially recognised since 2008); lawmakers from small conservative parties called it a 'provocation' while a same-sex civil union bill was pending — organised political opposition alongside official recognition.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the supreme court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. The capital has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below the worst regional levels.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2008 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2023 marriage ruling is a climate signal.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The surgery-required LGR process is resident-facing; the documented employment exclusion affects residents.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Surgery requirement for LGR and the marriage ruling are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation current overview: amendment of the general anti-discrimination law to include sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds was blocked by the national assembly in 2024 (claiming implicit coverage); no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes; intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited; at the 2025 UN universal periodic review multiple states urged explicit anti-discrimination protections, gender-recognition reform and stronger violence safeguards — legal reforms remain stalled and this country lags much of the region.

Rights-index data for this country: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment or housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage in regional polling (2023).

News outlet (16 Feb 2018): a supreme court justice withdrew his October 2017 draft ruling against marriage rights — the draft had held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while suggesting the assembly consider civil unions; the government signalled it would comply with the landmark 9 January 2018 regional human-rights court decision.

Broadcast features (14 Aug 2018): in an indigenous state/province of this country a flourishing local 'third gender' community is accepted as completely normal, with powerful matriarchal figures elevating women's status — cultural context for how gender diversity is received in this part of the country.

International LGBT-rights organisation current overview: anti-discrimination amendment blocked by the national assembly in 2024, no hate-crime recognition, unregulated intersex infant surgery, 2025 universal periodic review calls for sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections and gender-recognition reform — reforms stalled.

News outlet (22 Oct 2017): a reported supreme court justice's draft ruling found the family-code sections barring same-sex marriage 'not unconstitutional' while leaving the national assembly to legislate civil unions ('equality must be constitutionally guaranteed via the law'); the two marriage lawsuits (a foreign-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge) were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the first lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a national LGBTI action plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and an international human-rights expert on sexual orientation and gender identity conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. The capital hosts an annual Pride.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside the capital and along more conservative rural areas. Candidate status for the regional bloc is driving slow alignment.
rewrites.blindTangential: No sexual-orientation and gender-identity hate-crime statute, and discrimination in key areas drew the regional parliament's concern — relevant mainly to visitors who experience or witness bias incidents.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: There is no legal gender recognition (the country rejected a self-ID recommendation at its universal periodic review) — a resident-facing gap that does not affect a foreign passport holder.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Legal gender recognition absence and action-plan implementation gaps are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: End-of-mission statement of an international human-rights expert on sexual orientation and gender identity after the country visit to this country, 1-12 July 2024: assesses good practices and challenges and offers recommendations to the government — the international-review baseline for sexual-orientation and gender-identity conditions.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: discrimination complaints filed over the screenings of a film were mediated, with the commissioner ruling in favour in one case; a local LGBT organisation logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people; groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

UN report (17 Jun 2025) by the independent expert on the visit to this country of 1-12 Jul 2024: evaluates the country's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.

News outlet (Feb 5, 2010): the country passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation but without same-sex marriage; homosexuality had carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; the prime minister had voiced support for gay marriage in July 2009, framing the law as integration-driven.

Local news outlet (Jul 30, 2021): an opposition lawmaker attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda' — a record of parliamentary hostility toward LGBT education work.

Local news outlet (Jul 30, 2021): a lawmaker's social-media post branded the government 'LGBT' and accused it of pushing LGBT values in schools, illustrating political anti-LGBT messaging in the same week as the schools campaign row.

News outlet (Oct 27, 2011): the anti-discrimination commissioner reprimanded a ruling-party lawmaker for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors — the most advanced legal framework in its region. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), an anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and hate-crime provisions covering sexual orientation and gender identity; Pride in the capital proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by a regional LGBTI-rights organisation: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (per the regional commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, a small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution is advisable.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2020 same-sex partnership law — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: No legal gender recognition law (administrative practice inconsistent) — resident-facing; the misdemeanour-overuse practice affects resident victims.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Legal gender recognition inconsistency and prosecution-practice gaps are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new action plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI strategy was adopted; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.

International legal body's global legal history (updated 18 June 2026): this country appears among the 1977 regional cohort of decriminalisations; reference source for the decriminalisation date rather than country-specific analysis.

LGBT travel guide (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Pride in the capital was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people there. Dated but concrete on social climate.

News outlet (Oct 2013): the country's first Pride marched through the capital — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; a local LGBT organisation's representative said 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both official protection and organised hostility.

News outlet (2 Aug 2019): lawmakers blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — a regional LGBTI-rights organisation said LGBT people are 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 study found 51% of LGBT+ residents were closeted.

Local news outlet (Dec 2018): the government adopted the draft law on same-sex partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via a registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors — one of only five countries in the region still criminalising same-sex conduct (buggery carries life imprisonment on paper, though rarely enforced). A regional human-rights body heard evidence in November 2024 of severe violence against trans women: 69 cases of violence against trans women documented 2018–2022, in a country with a small population. Police fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence; there is no anti-discrimination legislation (an international human-rights body called for it in April 2024) and no legal gender recognition.

Cross-dressing was decriminalised after a 2018 regional court ruling, removing the most direct trans-expression statute, but the climate and investigative failure keep risk high. The capital has a small organised community.
rewrites.blindTangential: Buggery (life imprisonment on paper, rarely enforced) remains a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2018 regional court ruling struck cross-dressing laws.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Buggery statutes are rarely enforced (climate/situational); the regional court struck cross-dressing laws in 2018.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): this country is one of only five in the region still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct — criminal-law provisions on gross indecency, attempted buggery and buggery with life imprisonment, rarely enforced but fuelling stigma. Five of six parties in the 2025 election, including the ruling party, backed decriminalisation. The cross-dressing law was struck down in 2018 by a regional court ruling; no legal gender recognition; a 2022 poll found 72% acceptance, 13 points less hostility than in 2013.

Local news outlet (16 Nov 2024): at a regional human-rights body's session, a hearing — 'Impact of Gender-Based Violence on Migrant Women, Sex Workers, and Transgender Women' — heard testimony from three local organisations; the body's chair called on the country to take urgent action (the record's cited figure: 69 documented cases of violence against trans women 2018-2022).

Broadcast outlet (26 Mar 2017): a trans woman stabbed in the capital in January 2017, then told by a magistrate to 'dress like a man' and refused courtroom entry on 2 Mar — case dismissed. Turns on the 1893 cross-dressing offence (124 years old, 'improper purpose' open to magistrate interpretation). Documents both street violence and justice-system failure for trans residents.

Local news outlet (13 Nov 2018): a regional court of justice allowed the appeal of several trans women and struck the cross-dressing provision of the summary jurisdiction act as unconstitutionally vague and contrary to freedom of expression. Backdrop: 2009 arrests of trans women under the 1893 act with three nights' detention; the challenge filed in 2010 with a local LGBT organisation — removed the direct anti-cross-dressing offence.

News outlet (26 Mar 2017): corroborates the attack and the courtroom exclusion; a local LGBT organisation's leader calls the magistrate's conduct a 'dereliction of duty' while arguing that parliament, not courts, must repeal the 1893 law. Unique value: an LGBT-organisation response demanding legislative repeal.

Local news outlet (16 May 2019): a local LGBT organisation's leader documents police using residual summary jurisdiction clauses to extort LGBT people — men in 'compromising positions' threatened with arrest to extract bribes; same-sex couples harassed in public spaces; formal complainants face secondary discrimination at stations and give 'watered down' accounts. After the regional court ruling, loitering and vagrancy clauses remain usable against LGBT (mostly sex-worker) populations.
